fanoutqa_034438.x:
List of Apollo astronauts :: Astronauts who trained for Apollo but did not fly :: chunk_0010
* [L. Gordon Cooper Jr.](/wiki/Gordon_Cooper "Gordon Cooper") – from the Mercury Seven; veteran of Mercury *[Faith 7](/wiki/Faith_7 "Faith 7")* and commander of [Gemini 5](/wiki/Gemini_5 "Gemini 5"), was replaced as Apollo 14 commander by Alan Shepard and resigned from NASA in 1970.
* [Clifton C. "C.C." Williams Jr.](/wiki/Clifton_Williams "Clifton Williams") – from Group 3; was named as Schweickart's Lunar Module Pilot backup crew, but was killed when the [T-38](/wiki/Northrop_T-38_Talon "Northrop T-38 Talon") jet he was flying crashed near [Tallahassee, Florida](/wiki/Tallahassee,_Florida "Tallahassee, Florida") on October 5, 1967. He was replaced by Bean, who flew on [Apollo 12](/wiki/Apollo_12 "Apollo 12").
* [Vance D. Brand](/wiki/Vance_D._Brand "Vance D. Brand") – from Group 5; was on the support crew for Apollo 8 and Apollo 13; was named as Apollo 15 backup Command Module Pilot. Flew on the 1975 [Apollo–Soyuz Test Project](/wiki/Apollo%E2%80%93Soyuz_Test_Project "Apollo–Soyuz Test Project") (not a flight of the Apollo program). He also flew as commander of [STS-5](/wiki/STS-5 "STS-5"), [STS-41-B](/wiki/STS-41-B "STS-41-B") and [STS-35](/wiki/STS-35 "STS-35").
* [Edward G. Givens Jr.](/wiki/Edward_Givens "Edward Givens") – from Group 5; was on the support crew of Apollo 7, but died in a car crash near [Houston, Texas](/wiki/Houston,_Texas "Houston, Texas") on June 6, 1967.
* [Joe H. Engle](/wiki/Joe_Engle "Joe Engle") – from Group 5; was originally named as Apollo 17 Lunar Module Pilot, but lost his slot to Schmitt. After Apollo, he flew in the [Space Shuttle](/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") [Approach and Landing Tests](/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests"), then commanded [STS-2](/wiki/STS-2 "STS-2") and [STS-51-I](/wiki/STS-51-I "STS-51-I").

Main article: [List of people who flew to the Moon](/wiki/List_of_people_who_flew_to_the_Moon "List of people who flew to the Moon")

This decline did not stop until 1803, when the university was reestablished as a state-owned institution by [Karl Friedrich, Grand Duke of Baden](/wiki/Karl_Friedrich,_Grand_Duke_of_Baden "Karl Friedrich, Grand Duke of Baden"), to whom the part of the Palatinate situated on the right bank of the Rhine was allotted. Since then, the university bears his name together with the name of [Ruprecht I](/wiki/Rupert_I,_Elector_Palatine_of_the_Rhine "Rupert I, Elector Palatine of the Rhine"). Karl Friedrich divided the university into five faculties and placed himself at its head as rector, as did also his successors. During this decade, [Romanticism](/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") found expression in Heidelberg through [Clemens Brentano](/wiki/Clemens_Brentano "Clemens Brentano"), [Achim von Arnim](/wiki/Achim_von_Arnim "Achim von Arnim"), [Ludwig Tieck](/wiki/Ludwig_Tieck "Ludwig Tieck"), [Joseph Görres](/wiki/Joseph_G%C3%B6rres "Joseph Görres"), and [Joseph von Eichendorff](/wiki/Joseph_von_Eichendorff "Joseph von Eichendorff"), and there went forth a revival of the German [Middle Ages](/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages") in speech, poetry, and art.[[30]](#cite_note-ReferenceB-30)

The [City of Manchester Stadium](/wiki/City_of_Manchester_Stadium "City of Manchester Stadium") – the home of Manchester City since 2003

The City of Manchester Stadium in east Manchester, known as the Etihad Stadium since 2011 for sponsorship reasons, is on a 200-year [lease](/wiki/Lease "Lease") from [Manchester City Council](/wiki/Manchester_City_Council "Manchester City Council") to Manchester City. It has been the club's home since the end of the [2002–03 season](/wiki/2002%E2%80%9303_Manchester_City_F.C._season "2002–03 Manchester City F.C. season"), when City moved from [Maine Road](/wiki/Maine_Road "Maine Road").[[183]](#cite_note-187) Before moving to the stadium, the club spent in excess of £30 million to convert it to football use: the pitch was lowered, adding another tier of seating around it, and a new North Stand was constructed.[[184]](#cite_note-188) The inaugural match at the new stadium was a 2–1 win over [Barcelona](/wiki/FC_Barcelona "FC Barcelona") in a [friendly match](/wiki/Friendly_match "Friendly match").[[185]](#cite_note-189)

After playing home matches at five stadiums between 1880 and 1887, the club settled at [Hyde Road Football Stadium](/wiki/Hyde_Road_(stadium) "Hyde Road (stadium)"), its home for 36 years.[[186]](#cite_note-190) A fire destroyed the Main Stand in 1920, and the club moved to the 84,000 capacity Maine Road three years later. Maine Road, nicknamed the "Wembley of the North" by its designers, hosted the largest-ever crowd at an English club ground when 84,569 attended an [FA Cup](/wiki/1933%E2%80%9334_FA_Cup "1933–34 FA Cup") tie against Stoke City on 3 March 1934.[[187]](#cite_note-191) Though Maine Road was redeveloped several times over its 80-year lifespan, by 1995 its capacity was restricted to 32,000

The Food and Nutrition Board (FNB) of the U.S. [Institute of Medicine](/wiki/National_Academy_of_Medicine "National Academy of Medicine") has set Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDAs) for [essential amino acids](/wiki/Essential_amino_acid "Essential amino acid") in 2002. For adults 19 years and older, 19 mg of isoleucine/kg body weight is required daily.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

Beside its biological role as a nutrient, isoleucine also participates in regulation of [glucose](/wiki/Glucose "Glucose") metabolism.[[5]](#cite_note-Rajendram_2015-5) Isoleucine is an essential component of many proteins. As an essential amino acid, isoleucine must be ingested or protein production in the cell will be disrupted. [Fetal hemoglobin](/wiki/Fetal_hemoglobin "Fetal hemoglobin") is one of the many proteins that require isoleucine.[[12]](#cite_note-Honig_1967-12) Isoleucine is present in the gamma chain of fetal hemoglobin and must be present for the protein to form.[[12]](#cite_note-Honig_1967-12)

Genetic diseases can change the consumption requirements of isoleucine. Amino acids cannot be stored in the body. Buildup of excess amino acids will cause a buildup of toxic molecules so, humans have many pathways to degrade each amino acid when the need for protein synthesis has been met.[[13]](#cite_note-13) Mutations in isoleucine-degrading enzymes can lead to dangerous buildup of isoleucine and its toxic derivative. One example is [maple syrup urine disease (MSUD)](/wiki/Maple_syrup_urine_disease "Maple syrup urine disease"), a disorder that leaves people unable to breakdown isoleucine, [valine](/wiki/Valine "Valine"), and [leucine](/wiki/Leucine "Leucine").[[14]](#cite_note-14) People with MSUD manage their disease by a reduced intake of all three of those amino acids alongside drugs that help excrete built-up toxins.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

Many animals and plants are dietary sources of isoleucine as a component of proteins.[[5]](#cite_note-Rajendram_2015-5) Foods that have high amounts of isoleucine include [eggs](/wiki/Egg_as_food "Egg as food"), [soy protein](/wiki/Soy_protein "Soy protein"), [seaweed](/wiki/Seaweed "Seawee

The Chiefs in action in 1990

The Peoria Suns began play in 1983 when the [Danville Suns](/wiki/Danville_Suns "Danville Suns") relocated to Peoria from [Danville, Illinois](/wiki/Danville,_Illinois "Danville, Illinois").[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) They played their home games at [Meinen Field](/wiki/Shea_Stadium_(Peoria,_Illinois) "Shea Stadium (Peoria, Illinois)"), built in 1968, near the [Bradley University](/wiki/Bradley_University "Bradley University") campus. The team's name was changed to the Chiefs in 1984. The 1984 team was [managed](/wiki/Manager_(baseball) "Manager (baseball)") by future [Major League Baseball](/wiki/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball") manager [Joe Maddon](/wiki/Joe_Maddon "Joe Maddon").

The 1988 team, managed by future major league manager [Jim Tracy](/wiki/Jim_Tracy_(baseball) "Jim Tracy (baseball)"), was the subject of Joseph Bosco's book *The Boys Who Would Be Cubs*.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Meinen Field was renovated before the 1992 season and renamed Vonachen Stadium in honor of Chiefs owner [Pete Vonachen](/wiki/Pete_Vonachen "Pete Vonachen"). The team moved to [Dozer Park](/wiki/Dozer_Park "Dozer Park") in downtown Peoria on May 24, 2002. During the new park's first year, the team set a franchise attendance record of 254,407 and won the Midwest League championship.

Former Cubs catcher [Jody Davis](/wiki/Jody_Davis_(baseball) "Jody Davis (baseball)") managed the 2006 team.

[Baseball Hall of Famer](/wiki/National_Baseball_Hall_of_Fame_and_Museum "National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum") [Ryne Sandberg](/wiki/Ryne_Sandberg "Ryne Sandberg") was hired to manage the 2007 Chiefs, which went 71–68 and finished the second half 40–30 in a tie for the division title, but missed the playoff on a tiebreaker. The team set a new season attendance record of 259,794, an average of 3,800 per game. Sandberg returned to manage the Chiefs in 2008. Schumacher, who dominated the sport in the 1990s and early 2000s becoming in 1995 the youngest back-to-back World Champion at the time,[[475]](#cite_note-476)[[476]](#cite_note-477) was noted for his ability in the rain, winning many of the wet races he took part in,[[325]](#cite_note-Hilton_2003,_pp._131–132-326) most notably Spain in 1996,[[29]](#cite_note-Beer_2020-30) and for his race pace, being able to set consecutive qualifying fastest laps;[[318]](#cite_note-Auto_Racing_2007-319) due to refuelling, he missed out several pole positions, having set his race strategy through more fuel on board (from his debut in 1991 through to the end of 2002 before the introduction of race-fuel qualifying from 2003 onwards, Schumacher was only outqualified 13 times in 178 race entries), and won 23% more races than getting pole positions. He also respectively won 51 and 24 times without starting first or from the front row, and had 48 wins with fastest lap, all three being more than any other driver, and converted 40 of his pole positions to wins at 58%, a record number that was later beaten by Hamilton. By the time he first retired in 2006, with 91 wins in 248 starts out of 250 entries (only behind Patrese), Schumacher had a win ratio of 36% of starts, ahead of Senna and Prost, both of them at 25% of starts. He also had 27% of pole positions, 30% of fastest laps, and the most victories from pole with fastest lap (22).[[474]](#cite_note-Collantine_2006-475) He also could have won even more races had he joined the dominant teams of the 1990s (Williams and McLaren) and not joined Ferrari in 1996, a view echoed by his former teammate Irvine,[[477]](#cite_note-478) and could have become the first driver to win 100 races were it not for some situations outside his control, such as reliability issues causing him to finish lower than first in 1994, one revoked win in 1994, two collisions with Coulthard and Montoya in 1998 and 2004, the two wins he gave to Irvine and Barrichello in 1999 and 2002, and retirements at the 1993 Monaco Grand Prix, the 2006 Japanese Grand Prix, and the 2012 Monaco Grand

Casino Royale (2006 film) :: Release :: Cuts and censorship :: chunk_0014
*Casino Royale* was censored for its release in the UK, the US, Germany and China. In Britain, by omitting some of Le Chiffre's sadism and James Bond's reactions in the torture scene, the film received the desired [BBFC](/wiki/BBFC "BBFC") [12A rating](/wiki/12A_(British_Board_of_Film_Classification) "12A (British Board of Film Classification)").[[97]](#cite_note-98) In the United States, two fight scenes were censored to achieve a [PG-13](/wiki/PG-13_(Motion_Picture_Association) "PG-13 (Motion Picture Association)") rating: the fight between Bond and the traitorous MI6 agent Fisher's contact, and the fight between Bond and Obanno in the stairway at the Casino Royale.[[98]](#cite_note-DVD_Compare:_Casino_Royale-99)

The German edit of the film cuts a sequence where the bomb-planter at the airport breaks a man's neck, instead replacing it with an alternative take.[[98]](#cite_note-DVD_Compare:_Casino_Royale-99) The mainland Chinese cut of the film also trims the torture scene and the stairway fight, as well as a shot of Bond cleaning his wound at the hotel and a boat scene.

The fully uncensored version can be found on the Australian, Dutch, French, Hong Kong, Japanese and Scandinavian Blu-ray and DVD releases, on UK Blu-ray releases from 2012 onwards (rated 15), and on the 4K UHD Blu-ray release (branded as an unrated "extended" cut).

AlphaGo (white) won the first game. Lee appeared to be in control throughout the match, but AlphaGo gained the advantage in the final 20 minutes, and Lee resigned.[[45]](#cite_note-bbc_9_March_2016-45) Lee stated afterwards that he had made a critical error at the beginning of the match; he said that the computer's strategy in the early part of the game was "excellent" and that the AI had made one unusual move that no human Go player would have made.[[45]](#cite_note-bbc_9_March_2016-45) David Ormerod, commenting on the game at Go Game Guru, described Lee's seventh stone as "a strange move to test AlphaGo's strength in the opening", characterising the move as a mistake and AlphaGo's response as "accurate and efficient". He described AlphaGo's position as favourable in the first part of the game, considering that Lee started to come back with move 81 before making "questionable" moves at 119 and 123, followed by a "losing" move at 129.[[46]](#cite_note-Gogameguru_9_March_2016-46) Professional Go player [Cho Hanseung](/wiki/Cho_Hanseung "Cho Hanseung") commented that AlphaGo's game had greatly improved from when it beat [Fan Hui](/wiki/Fan_Hui "Fan Hui") in October 2015.[[46]](#cite_note-Gogameguru_9_March_2016-46) Michael Redmond described the computer's game as being more aggressive than against Fan.[[47]](#cite_note-47)

According to 9-dan Go grandmaster Kim Seong-ryong, Lee seemed stunned by AlphaGo's strong play on the 102nd stone.[[48]](#cite_note-hani.co.kr-48) After watching AlphaGo make the game's 102nd move, Lee mulled over his options for more than 10 minutes.[[48]](#cite_note-hani.co.kr-48)

Main article: [Venues of the 2012 Summer Olympics and Paralympics](/wiki/Venues_of_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_and_Paralympics "Venues of the 2012 Summer Olympics and Paralympics")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/London_Queen_Elizabeth_Olympic_Park.jpg/250px-London_Queen_Elizabeth_Olympic_Park.jpg)](/wiki/File:London_Queen_Elizabeth_Olympic_Park.jpg)

The [Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park](/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_Olympic_Park "Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park")

The 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games used a mixture of new venues, existing and historic facilities, and temporary facilities, some of them in well-known locations such as [Hyde Park](/wiki/Hyde_Park,_London "Hyde Park, London") and [Horse Guards Parade](/wiki/Horse_Guards_Parade "Horse Guards Parade"). After the Games, some of the new facilities would be reused in their Olympic form, while others were resized or relocated.[[41]](#cite_note-44)

The majority of venues were divided into three zones within [Greater London](/wiki/Greater_London "Greater London"): the Olympic Zone, the River Zone and the Central Zone. In addition there were a few venues that, by necessity, were outside the boundaries of Greater London, such as the [Weymouth and Portland National Sailing Academy](/wiki/Weymouth_and_Portland_National_Sailing_Academy "Weymouth and Portland National Sailing Academy") some 125 mi (201 km) southwest of London, which hosted the [sailing](/wiki/Sailing_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics "Sailing at the 2012 Summer Olympics") events. The football tournament was staged at several grounds around the UK.[[42]](#cite_note-45) Work began on the Park in December 2006, when a sports hall in [Eton Manor](/wiki/Eton_Manor "Eton Manor") was pulled down.[[43]](#cite_note-46) The athletes' village in Portland was completed in September 2011.[[44]](#cite_note-47)

The name *Alaska* ([Russian](/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): Аля́ска, [romanized](/wiki/Romanization_of_Russian "Romanization of Russian"): *Aljáska*) was introduced during the [Russian colonial period](/wiki/Russian_America "Russian America") when it was used to refer to the [Alaska Peninsula](/wiki/Alaska_Peninsula "Alaska Peninsula"). It was derived from an [Aleut-language](/wiki/Aleut_language "Aleut language") idiom, *alaxsxaq*, meaning 'the mainland' or, more literally, 'the object towards which the action of the sea is directed'.[[10]](#cite_note-Aleut-11)[[11]](#cite_note-Bright-12)[[12]](#cite_note-13)
